primary_source.title: A Multilab Preregistered Replication of the Ego-Depletion Effect

review_method: Downloaded the version of record from the authors' copy at https://www.dominique.muller.lippc2s.fr/resources/documents/HCetal_2016_PPS.pdf and read it page by page. This machine has no poppler or PDF library, so each page's Flate-compressed content stream was decompressed with zlib and its show-text operators collected, then matched on space-normalized text because the typesetting kerns words apart ("ef f ec t"). Page numbers come from each page's printed running head, so every locator below is the printed page, not a PDF index. Verified on 2026-11-03: the k = 23 / N = 2,141 pair on pp. 546 and 551, d = 0.04 with the 95% CI on pp. 546 and 554, the d = 0.62 / 198-test sentence on p. 547, and the three-dissenting-labs sentence on p. 554.

claims.paraphrase: 23 laboratories ran the same preregistered ego-depletion protocol on 2,141 participants.
claims.support_summary: Abstract, p. 546: "Multiple laboratories (k = 23, total N = 2,141) conducted replications of a standardized ego-depletion protocol based on a sequential-task paradigm by Sripada et al." The same k and N are repeated in Results, p. 551: "Sample demographics and results for each of the participating labs (k = 23, total N = 2,141) are provided in Table 1 for the depletion and no-depletion conditions."

claims.paraphrase: Pooled across the labs the effect was d = 0.04, 95% CI -0.07 to 0.15, an interval that includes zero, so the second-task deficit was small.
claims.support_summary: Abstract, p. 546: "the size of the ego-depletion effect was small with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) that encompassed zero (d = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.15]." Restated in the meta-analysis results, p. 554: "Averaged sample-weighted effect sizes for the mean RTV (d = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.07, 0.15]) and RT (d = 0.04, 95% CI [-0.07 to 0.14]) variables were small and confidence intervals included the value of zero." The measure is reaction-time variability on the incongruent trials of the second task (p. 551), so the burned-in "THE 0.04 RESULT" card names the pooled figure, not a per-lab one.

claims.paraphrase: An earlier meta-analysis averaged d = 0.62 across 198 tests of the ego-depletion effect.
claims.support_summary: Introduction, p. 547: "An initial meta-analysis revealed a medium effect size (d = 0.62) across 198 tests of the ego-depletion effect (Hagger, Wood, Stiff, & Chatzisarantis, 2010a)." The same page records that "recent conceptual and empirical analyses have challenged the resource depletion explanation" and "questioned the strength of the ego-depletion effect or whether it exists at all", which is what the Short contrasts against 0.04.

claims.paraphrase: Three of the 23 replications returned an interval that excluded zero, one of them negative.
claims.support_summary: p. 554: "In terms of individual labs' data, only three of the 23 replications did not have 95% confidence intervals for the ego-depletion effect size that included zero for RTV, and one of those was negative (i.e., in the opposite direction to the hypothesized ego-depletion effect). Similarly, only three labs found mean RT values with confidence intervals that did not include the value of zero, two of which were negative." Recorded because it is the reason the narration says "pooled" rather than "across all labs", which the earlier draft of this dossier asserted.

editorial_suggestions.text: "You waste your morning believing willpower runs out" is the channel's framing of a popular self-help claim. The study ran a letter-inhibition task in a laboratory session; no morning, and no time-of-day measure, appears in the paper.
editorial_suggestions.status: creator editorial, not a finding of Hagger & Chatzisarantis (2016)

editorial_suggestions.text: "'willpower runs out by noon' keeps being reprinted" names a cultural pattern, not a measured effect. The only figure in that scene that traces to the paper is the 198 tests on p. 547.
editorial_suggestions.status: creator editorial, not a finding of Hagger & Chatzisarantis (2016)

editorial_suggestions.text: The "five-second reframe" in the closing ask is this channel's own device. Hagger & Chatzisarantis (2016) tested no reframe, no intervention and no five-second anything, so no effect is claimed for it; the video offers it as a prompt, not as evidence.
editorial_suggestions.status: creator editorial, not a finding of Hagger & Chatzisarantis (2016)

primary_source.title: A Multilab Preregistered Replication of the Ego-Depletion Effect

dossier.experiment_design: Preregistered replication run by 23 laboratories on 2,141 participants: each lab ran the same sequential-task protocol, an initial self-control task followed by a Stroop-style incongruent trial block, with reaction-time variability as the primary measure.
dossier.stat_subtitle: Pooled Ego-Depletion Effect (Hagger et al. 2016, p. 546)
dossier.comparison_text: the pooled effect was *d = 0.04*—a confidence interval that spans zero—against the *d = 0.62* averaged across 198 earlier tests
dossier.broken_assumption: You act like willpower is a tank the last hour drained—23 labs ran that test and the second task barely noticed.
dossier.biological_mechanism: Pooled across the labs, the second-task deficit was small and its confidence interval included zero.
dossier.real_world_tax: It is why 'willpower runs out by noon' keeps being reprinted: 198 tests made it sound settled.
dossier.willpower_trap: Belief keeps the advice alive; the pooled 0.04 is what the protocol returned.
dossier.five_second_override: The *five-second* reframe? Name the task in front of you, not the tank you assume is empty. Comment below which task you blame on willpower.
dossier.best_hook: You waste your morning believing willpower runs out—23 labs tested it on 2,141 people; here is the result.
dossier.loop_bridge: Because the moment a null result gets reprinted as a law of willpower...
